title_original: ‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
editorial_title_zh: 同性Mumblegore鬼故事《Sinner Supper Club》由Factory 25买下
editorial_excerpt_zh: 该片用iPhone历时6天拍摄完成，将在NewFest上首映。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "总部位于布鲁克林的独立电影发行公司Factory 25在NewFest的纽约首映式上，取得了黛西·罗萨托（Daisy Rosato）与诺拉·凯伊（Nora Kaye）的长片处女作《Sinner Supper Club》的全球版权。影片被描述为一个“同性mumblegore鬼故事”，讲述了一群朋友重新聚在一起，为因被高昂生活成本挤出纽约市而离开的吉纳维芙（Genevieve）举办“守灵夜”的故事。随着夜色渐深，热浪将他们困在一起，他们长期被忽视的问题彻底爆发……接着，他们死去的朋克朋友出现了。", "links": [{"text": "Factory 25", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/factory-25/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "NewFest", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/newfest/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片通过即兴创作，用iPhone历时6天拍摄完成。它是对以mumblegore和Dogme 95运动为特征的粗粝、实验性电影制作的致敬。作为制作的一部分，电影制作人撰写了一份宣言，探讨了在2020年代制作电影意味着什么，其中的角色代表了酷儿、跨性别以及性别不具规范性（gender nonconforming）的社群。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/china-fully-ai-movie-box-office-convert.io_.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "《三星堆：未来与过去》", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_A1552_febcc6.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Dzifa Yador、Jax Clark与Ali Foreman于2026年10月17日在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶Lumen举办的IndieWire电影制作未来峰会上。", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "演员阵容包括爱丽丝·吉布勒（Elise Kibler）、阿希尔·李（Ashil Lee）、吉纳维芙·西蒙（Genevieve Simon）、杰亚·莱利二世（Jayae Riley Jr.）、苏菲·萨根-古瑟茨（Sophie Sagan-Gutherz）、凯伊和罗萨托。除了执导并在片中出演外，凯伊和罗萨托还共同撰写了剧本。罗萨托同时担任摄影指导。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Factory 25计划于2027年春季在院线上映该片，随后进行数字发行和蓝光发行。Factory 25曾发行过《Funny Ha Ha》、《Ham on Rye》、《Happer’s Comet》、《Actual People》、《This Closeness》、《Family Portrait》和《Queens of the Qing Dynasty》等电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "NewFest于1988年为应对艾滋病危机而创立。这个纽约LGBTQ+电影节一直是纽约市酷儿文化场景的重要支柱。在此后的几年里，NewFest已扩展成为一个电影与媒体组织，开展全年项目以服务LGBTQ+社群的各个方面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "以下是该片的预告片：", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Factory 25 , a Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired worldwide rights to Daisy Rosato and Nora Kaye’s first feature film “Sinner Supper Club” at the New York premiere of the film at NewFest . article_text:
Factory 25 , a Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired worldwide rights to Daisy Rosato and Nora Kaye’s first feature film “Sinner Supper Club” at the New York premiere of the film at NewFest . The film is described as a “gay mumblegore ghost story” about friends reuniting to throw a “wake” for Genevieve, who has been priced out of New York City. As the night progresses and a heatwave traps them together, their long-ignored problems boil over….and then their dead friend shows up.

The film was shot in six days on an iPhone through improvisation. It is an homage to the scrappy and experimental filmmaking that characterized both the mumblegore and Dogme 95 movements. As part of production, the filmmakers wrote a manifesto, one that explored what it means to make a film in the 2020’s, with characters that represent the queer and transgender and gender nonconforming community.

The cast includes Elise Kibler, Ashil Lee, Genevieve Simon, Jayae Riley Jr., Sophie Sagan-Gutherz, Kaye and Rosato. In addition to directing and appearing in the film, Kaye and Rosato wrote the screenplay. Rosato also served as the cinematographer.

Factory 25 is planning a spring 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital and Blu-ray release. Factory 25 has released such films as “Funny Ha Ha,” “Ham on Rye,” “Happer’s Comet,” “Actual People,” “This Closeness,” “Family Portrait,” and “Queens of the Qing Dynasty.”

NewFest was founded in 1988 in response to the AIDS crisis. The New York LGBTQ+ Film Festival has been a tentpole of NYC’s queer cultural scene. In the subsequent years, NewFest has expanded into a film and media organization with year-long programs to serve all facets of the LGBTQ+ community.

article_text:
Light and Magic is the first major exhibition to explore pictorialism as a global movement. Discover how artists became pioneers of the darkroom, transforming our understanding of photography and image making.

Bringing together over 200 rare prints by over 80 artists from Seoul to Sydney, New York to Cape Town and Brazil to Singapore, this truly international exhibition takes a fresh and inclusive look at the history of photography.

Featuring never-before seen works from around the world alongside pieces from Tate’s Collection, Light and Magic highlights the vast and varied artistic possibilities of photography as a medium.

Light and Magic is presented in the Eyal Ofer Galleries.

Seasonal dining and Light and Magic

Enjoy lunch or dinner after the exhibition

Experience the exhibition then enjoy two courses from our set menu, which focuses on bold, seasonal British dishes with a commitment to sustainable sourcing and simple, thoughtful cooking.

Choose a time slot that includes lunch, dinner or a cocktail when booking your exhibition ticket. The time slot you book will be when you enter the exhibition.

Members can reserve a table here .

Exhibition with lunch or dinner

£59 for exhibition entry followed by two courses from our seasonal set menu

Choose the 10.45, 11.15, 12.45 or 13.15 time slot to book your exhibition visit with lunch. For dinner, the time slots are on Fridays and Saturdays only at 17.15, 17.45, 18.15 and 18.45*.

The time slot is when you will go into the exhibition, your table in the Restaurant will be reserved for 1 hour and 15 minutes later. Please note the last seating time is 14.45 for lunch, and 20.00 for dinner. Final orders will be taken 15 minutes after this time.

We have vegan, vegetarian and gluten free options available. If you have any additional requirements or allergies, please notify the team in advance at restaurant@tate.org.uk so we can best accommodate you on the day.

Light and Magic is on Level 3 of the Natalie Bell Building and the Restaurant is a few floors above, on Level 6.

*This offer runs until 3 January 2027. It is not available on 23, 24, 30 and 31 October and 28 November 2026.

Smartphone audio guide

Hear from curators and artists as they tell the untold global story of art photography showcased in Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography .

Get closer to the art with this self-guided audio tour on your smartphone.

After purchase, you’ll receive an exclusive link to your audio guide via email. Open the link at the exhibition entrance and listen using your own headphones or your smartphone speaker. No headphones or physical audio devices are provided at the gallery.

Add the £5 guide when booking your ticket. Already a Member? Purchase your guide .

Exhibition guide

Discover more about Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography and five artworks not to miss with our exhibition guide.

Accessibility

Need a larger size of the exhibition wall texts? Download the large print guide [PDF].

All Tate Modern entrances are step-free. You can enter via the Turbine Hall and into the Natalie Bell Building on Holland Street, or into the Blavatnik Building on Sumner street. There are lifts to every floor of the Blavatnik and Natalie Bell buildings. Alternatively you can take the stairs.

Fully accessible toilets are located on every floor on the concourses

A quiet room is available to use in the Natalie Bell Building on Level 4

Ear defenders can be borrowed from the Ticket desks

To help plan your visit to Tate Modern, have a look at our visual story . It includes photographs and information about what you can expect from a visit to the gallery. Download Tate Modern map For more information before your visit:

Email hello@tate.org.uk

Call +44 (0)20 7887 8888 (daily 10.00–17.00)

article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 23.

Thomas Mann, Nobel Prize-winning writer and voice of the German resistance from abroad, fled Germany in 1933 to take refuge in California, where he lived for sixteen years before returning to Germany in 1949 to receive the Goethe Prize in Frankfurt, show face, and embrace the flattery of his snowballing celebrity. That’s where we enter Polish writer-director (and for the first time, editor) Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , a film that traces Mann’s (Hanns Zischler) widely publicized but brief return to his homeland under the guidance of his brilliant, staid daughter and translator Erika (Sandra Hüller).

We open in Cannes and watch a long conversation unfold between Erika and her brother Klaus (August Diehl) about the approaching tour of their father. Pawlikowski, who was nominated for a Best Directing Oscar for Cold War , makes the captivating decision to keep the camera on Klaus throughout the whole call, only revealing Erika when they say their goodbyes. From there, Klaus is rarely seen again, and Erika and Thomas take center stage, occupying every stunning composition with what seems the weight of the world on their shoulders, thematically transferred from the “life-weary, drug addict” Klaus.

Erika and Thomas start in Frankfurt, West Germany, where the novelist accepts his award and confronts an international press that both praises and grills him. Later they road-trip to the ideologically opposite Weimar in the east, crossing a divided fatherland and leaving an inky black trail of tension, narcissism, and intimate familial pain in their wake.

When asked why he “abandoned” his people during such a difficult time, Thomas sternly remarks that he wouldn’t be alive if he hadn’t. But that doesn’t satisfy his most scathing critics. No matter what you come in knowing or not knowing, any viewer will quickly understand that Mann is an incredibly controversial figure and his return to Germany both maligned and adored. Some find him persona non grata; others line the streets waiting for his arrival like he’s Elvis.

For how accessible Pawlikowski’s previous two features were, Fatherland feels like it’s made by someone else. The trademark black-and-white cinematography (so elegant it almost feels marbled) from regular collaborator Łukasz Żal points to Pawlikowski, as does the tight 82-minute runtime and squarish, 1.37:1 aspect ratio. In a way, Fatherland is also the third in what amounts to a World War II trilogy. But the subject, flow, and approachability combine for the coming of a new Pawlikowski in heady academic form—an auteur in the shape of a wizened professor, much like Mann.

It’s the kind of project that will alienate many viewers by the first Mann press conference in Frankfurt, where it becomes immediately clear that a lack of knowledge surrounding the historical events in question–which range from microscopically inside-baseball to sweepingly applicable to any nationalist bent across the globe–will render a litany of references and conversations impenetrable for anyone without a PhD on the subject.

The screenplay (co-written by Henk Handloegten) deals heavily with prominent philosophers like Kant and Nietzsche, references a love for Wagner as an alignment with Hitler, and dives headfirst into the controversy of Mann’s presence in Germany that consumes the split country in the immediate aftermath of the war. Here, something as simple as a boys’ choir singing a nationalist anthem has such a strong undercurrent of historical context that it deserves serious investigation to pick up on why we’re seeing it, whereas in Cold War , the undercurrent in the choir is there, but understanding the unwieldy history beneath the frame is much less integral to following the devastating love story at the film’s core.

That said, Pawlikowski is a master of making the viewer feel (at times, even mysteriously understand) what emotion or psychology lies beneath the surface of the image, and the complex, contentious feeling of Fatherland is contagious more often than not. Who can’t relate to being frustrated with a parent? Or, at the very least, an infinitely complex relation to a parent that reflects love, resentment, and a lifetime spent together? That contagious feeling hurts because everyone in Fatherland is hurting.

One might not be fully clued in on the historical or philosophical reference being discussed at every turn, but they can feel Erika’s admiration and disdain for her father, Klaus’s existential aimlessness in the wake of the Third Reich’s reign, and Thomas’s grating obsession with himself. It’s the kind of film you ache through. But the aching doesn’t come from devastating romance or impossible love, as it did in Cold War , but the inherent difficulty in ever fully grasping one’s identity or coming to terms with the inevitable conflict of family.

Regular collaborator Joanna Kulig has a delightful cameo as a jazz singer. She also probably would’ve knocked the Erika part out of the park, but it’s hard to imagine anyone playing the incredibly subtle, emotionally tangled, and sophisticated part of Erika better than Sanda Hüller, the German-born actress who’s been on an absolute roll since 2023, when she co-led two modern greats in The Zone of Interest and Anatomy of a Fall and attracted the attention of non-cinephilic audiences with an Oscar nomination for the latter that landed her in her first American blockbuster ( Project Hail Mary ). In the international cinema scene, that streak started a decade ago with Toni Erdmann , another film about a daughter who must tolerate a tone-deaf father, this one much funnier than Thomas Mann.

For how quickly it passes, the dense, cleverly titled Fatherland ––a nod to the nationalist German “Vaterland” and cheeky framing of the father-daughter story it tells––is about so much: heimat/belonging, the disappearance of meaning (“Do you believe in anything anymore? Maybe we should all just kill ourselves.”), collective and individual guilt, inherited pain, “a spiritual and moral future,” and the sometimes impossible task of clearing one’s conscience politically, societally, and/or personally. While it doesn’t clear the bar of his last two (it’s hard to be better than perfect), Fatherland is Pawlikowski in immaculate form. Successive watches will no doubt reveal greater and greater depths to behold, the film all but guaranteed to age like a fine wine.

Fatherland premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当代际流传的知识转化为崭新的事物时，会发生什么？在“神圣红树林”（The Sacred Mangrove）中，巴哈马艺术家阿妮娜·梅杰（Anina Major）通过纪念碑式的陶瓷雕塑重新构想了传统的棕榈编织，创造了一个审视记忆、移民与文化延续性的沉浸式景观。梅杰汲取了祖母传下来的编织技艺，挑战了工艺与纯艺术之间的界限，同时对文化价值如何被赋予和保存提出了质疑。通过编织的黏土结构、瓶树以及对加勒比海生态的呼应，该展览审视了祖先渊源、劳作、灵性与归属感之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在接受《ART AFRICA》采访时，梅杰反思了传统实践中持久的智慧、巴哈马身份表达的复杂性，以及文化知识如何在世代和地域之间不断演变。“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-14.54.42.png", "alt": "", "caption": "“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布伦登·贝尔-罗伯茨（Brendon Bell-Roberts）：“神圣红树林”的核心在于你将编织这种有机、灵活的实践转化为通过烧制黏土成型的过程。当你把一种与无常相关的物质传统转化为某种持久的东西时，哪些可能得以实现？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿妮娜·梅杰（Anina Major）：我发现永恒与无常之间的关系非常迷人，因为这两种材料都不是绝对的非此即彼。棕榈是有机的，最终会生物降解，而黏土在经历火的非凡蜕变之前，最初是柔软而脆弱的。它变得永恒，却依然脆弱。最初，与黏土合作是我在祖母去世后保持与她联系的一种方式。我看着她留下的仅有的几件草编物品慢慢变质，开始好奇如果将这些手势转化为另一种材料会发生什么。浮现出来的远不止是保存一种形式的方式。黏土为尺度、结构和表达带来了它自己的可能性。它让我重新审视我们如何看待这些熟悉的物品，以及我们赋予其中蕴含知识的价值。通过“神圣红树林”，这种探索已经从个别雕塑扩展到了整个景观。“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.33-1030x684.png", "alt": "", "caption": "“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴哈马文化中，编织承载着劳作、知识与祖先的历史。在你的实践中，你是如何对待这些历史的，特别是当面对在代际间不断演变的传统时？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我是在身边的女性、尤其是祖母的影响下理解编织的。这是她日常生活的一部分，是一项需要耐心、创造力和对材料惊人理解的技能。当我开始更深入地研究这一实践时，我开始对双手传达了多少知识产生兴趣。编织兼具数学性、结构性、经济性和文化性。图案中蕴含着历史，但这些图案的诠释方式也具有巨大的个性。每一代人都在做出自己的贡献，无论是通过材料、技术还是用途的变化。我的作品也是对那场持续对话的又一次贡献。阿妮娜·梅杰，“水塔”（Water Tower），2024年。上釉炻器、熔融海玻璃与沙子。佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆收藏，由PAMM收藏家委员会提供资金购藏。鸣谢阿妮娜·梅杰。图片由艺术家与特恩画廊（Tern Gallery）提供。摄影：安德鲁·怀特（Andrew White）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/WaterTower3_AMajor-663x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "阿妮娜·梅杰，“水塔”（Water Tower），2024年。上釉炻器、熔融海玻璃与沙子。佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆收藏，由PAMM收藏家委员会提供资金购藏。鸣谢阿妮娜·梅杰。图片由艺术家与特恩画廊（Tern Gallery）提供。摄影：安德鲁·怀特（Andrew White）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览探讨了文化传统与巴哈马在旅游经济中形象表现之间的关系。这种张力是如何塑造你对作品中的价值、可见度与文化身份的思考的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴哈马长大期间，旅游业是我们理解自我以及世界其余部分如何看待我们时不可避免的一部分。天堂的形象具有难以置信的力量，但它也可能扁平化一个地方及其居民的复杂性。在草编市场（Straw Market）作为纪念品出售的编织物能够体现出非凡的历史和精湛的技艺。在另一个语境中，关于其价值的对话发生了转变。正是这种论述启发了这批作品。它质疑了那些决定我们庆祝什么、忽视什么以及承认谁的贡献的体制。“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.09-683x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "“阿妮娜·梅杰：神圣红树林”展览现场，佩雷斯迈阿密艺术博物馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚内斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "红树林在加勒比海生态系统中占据着重要空间，它们存在于陆地与水域之间，同时提供保护、庇护和相互关联的生命系统。是什么吸引你将红树林作为本次展览的框架，它在作品中承载着怎样的含义？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在构思“The Sacred Mangrove”时，我把这片景观既视作物理环境，也视作那些相互关联的支持、保护和转化系统的隐喻。红树林是那种抗拒简单定义的生态系统。它们存在于陆地与水域之间，不断适应着变化的环境，却支撑着极其复杂的生命系统。根系相互交织，形成了既能提供保护和稳定、又能让其他生命形式繁衍的结构。这难道不能为我们思考文化传统如何延续提供另一种方式吗？它们不一定是通过保持不变而存续，而是通过适应、交流以及维持它们的种种关系。‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘展览现场，佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.21-684x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘展览现场，佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "装置汇集了高耸的编织陶艺形态、瓶树（bottle trees）、碎海螺壳以及 Water Tower 。这些物件与材料在展览空间中是如何彼此对话的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我将这次展览视为一片风景，而非孤立雕塑的集合。每一个元素都对这个环境有所贡献，它们之间的关系与物件本身同样重要。高耸的陶瓷结构确立了一种纪念碑式的质感，而瓶树则带入了非洲大 diaspora（海外族裔）中有关保护和精神实践的联想。碎海螺壳和陶瓷碎片则增添了隐喻意义，使作品不再仅仅依托于一个展示雕塑的表面。Water Tower 取材自拿骚与水和维持生计相关的历史地标。在展览中，它与周围的形态建立起了另一种关系。我感兴趣的是，这些不同的元素如何开始营造出一种场所感，而不一定非要代表某个特定的地点。它们共同暗示了一种由劳作、生存、灵性历史以及我们与自然世界的关系所塑造的环境。阿妮娜·梅杰（Anina Major），‘ Water Tower ‘，2024年。釉面炻器、熔融海玻璃与沙子。佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆藏，由 PAMM 收藏家委员会提供资金购自博物馆。鸣谢阿妮娜·梅杰。图片由艺术家与特恩画廊（Tern Gallery）提供。摄影：安德鲁·怀特（Andrew White）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.05.13-664x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "阿妮娜·梅杰（Anina Major），‘ Water Tower ‘，2024年。釉面炻器、熔融海玻璃与沙子。佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆藏，由 PAMM 收藏家委员会提供资金购自博物馆。鸣谢阿妮娜·梅杰。图片由艺术家与特恩画廊（Tern Gallery）提供。摄影：安德鲁·怀特（Andrew White）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的创作游走于通常被分开归类的工艺、雕塑和装置等范畴之间。你如何看待自己作品中的这些区别，当它们重叠时会发生什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在创作时，我很少去想我的作品究竟属于工艺、雕塑还是装置。这些区分对创作过程来说往往感觉相当束缚。编织凝聚了非凡的智慧，然而那些与女性、家务劳作或主流艺术史之外的社群相关的实践，却往往被赋予了不同的归类。我很好奇，当这些等级制度受到挑战时会发生什么，尤其是在材料和体量方面。我最欣赏的一些物件和艺术品模糊了这些界限，历史也表明，物件可以根据观看者是谁、在何处呈现以及在何时呈现而在不同类别之间转换。我的创作已从单一的陶瓷雕塑演变为与景观互动的环境。我不认为这是将工艺抛在脑后。相反，我想看看编织的结构语言究竟能延伸到多远，以及在此过程中会涌现出哪些新的可能性。‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘展览现场，佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.46-687x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘展览现场，佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆，2026年。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "记忆与归属感的概念贯穿于你的整个创作。在巴哈马和纽约两地生活和工作的经历，是如何塑造你对地点、距离以及文化知识的保存或转化的理解的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "离开巴哈马让我更加意识到地点是如何塑造我们对自身的理解的。有些东西当你被它们包围时会觉得理所当然，而距离有一种魔力，能让这些东西变得清晰。但远离故土也让你的归属关系变得复杂。你变了，你离开的地方也变了，最终你会认识到，回归并不意味着能完全找回记忆中的原貌。这种经历影响了我对文化 traditions（传统）的看法。要完好无损地保存过去或许是不可能的，但当人们在不同地方辗转并遭遇各种影响时，它将如何继续演变——这才是引人入胜之处。阿妮娜·梅杰肖像。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.59-682x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "阿妮娜·梅杰肖像。摄影：拉扎罗·利亚尼斯（Lazaro Llanes）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当观众以身体切实穿行于‘ The Sacred Mangrove ‘之中时，他们与该装置的体量、物质性和空间布局的遭遇，在作品的展开过程中扮演了什么角色？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "以更大的尺度进行创作，从根本上改变了我与作品的关系。面对较小的物件时，这种接触可以相当私密。你站在作品之外去观察它。但一个环境对你提出了不同的要求。你必须在空间中进行物理上的穿梭，在周围和其间移动。在“The Sacred Mangrove”中，雕塑的排列、其下方的地面以及它们之间的空隙，都是体验的一部分。观者的身体成了衡量作品的尺度，而他们的移动也随着他们所注意到的事物而改变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次展览目前正在位于佛罗里达州的佩雷斯艺术博物馆迈阿密分馆展出，展期至2027年8月1日。", "links": [{"text": "Pérez Art Museum Miami", "url": "https://www.pamm.org/en/exhibition/anina-major-the-sacred-mangrove/"}], "translated": true}]

In ‘The Sacred Mangrove ‘ , Bahamian artist Anina Major reimagines traditional palm weaving through monumental ceramic sculptures, creating an immersive landscape that considers memory, migration and cultural continuity. Drawing on the plaiting practices passed down by her grandmother, Major challenges the distinctions between craft and fine art while questioning how cultural value is assigned and preserved. Through woven clay structures, bottle trees and references to Caribbean ecologies, the exhibition examines the relationships between ancestry, labour, spirituality and belonging."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In conversation with ART AFRICA , Major reflects on the enduring intelligence of traditional practices, the complexities of representing Bahamian identity, and how cultural knowledge continues to evolve across generations and geographies. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-14.54.42.png", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Brendon Bell-Roberts: At the centre of ‘The Sacred Mangrove’ is your transformation of weaving from an organic, flexible practice into one shaped through fired clay. What becomes possible when you translate a material tradition associated with impermanence into something enduring?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Anina Major: I find the relationship between permanence and impermanence fascinating because neither material is entirely one or the other. Palm is organic and eventually biodegrades, while clay begins soft and vulnerable before undergoing an extraordinary transformation through fire. It becomes permanent, yet remains fragile. Initially, working with clay was a way of maintaining a connection to my grandmother after her passing. I was watching the few straw objects she left behind slowly deteriorate, and I became curious about what might happen if I translated those gestures into another material. What emerged was more than a way of preserving a form. Clay introduced its own possibilities for scale, structure, and expression. It allowed me to reconsider how we encounter these familiar objects and the value we assign to the knowledge embedded within them. With ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, that exploration has expanded beyond individual sculptures into an entire landscape. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.33-1030x684.png", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Weaving carries histories of labour, knowledge and ancestry within Bahamian culture. How do you approach these histories in your practice, especially when working with traditions that continue to evolve across generations?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I grew up understanding plaiting through the women around me, particularly my grandmother. It was part of her everyday life, a skill that required patience, ingenuity, and an incredible understanding of material. As I began researching the practice more deeply, I became interested in how much knowledge was being communicated through the hands. Plaiting is mathematical, structural, economic, and cultural all at once. There are histories embedded in the patterns, but there is also tremendous individuality in how those patterns are interpreted. Every generation makes its own contributions, whether through changes in material, technique, or purpose. My work is another contribution to that ongoing conversation. How has this tension shaped how you think about value, visibility and cultural identity in your work?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Growing up in The Bahamas, tourism was an unavoidable part of how we understood ourselves and how the rest of the world encountered us. The image of paradise is incredibly powerful, but it can also flatten the complexity of a place and the people who inhabit it. A plaited object sold in the Straw Market as a souvenir had the ability to embody extraordinary history and skill. Within another context, the conversation around its value shifts. It’s this discourse that inspired this body of work. Questioning the systems that determine what we celebrate, what we overlook, and whose contributions are recognised. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-12.04.09-683x1030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mangroves occupy an important space within Caribbean ecologies, existing between land and water while providing protection, shelter and interconnected systems of life. What drew you to the mangrove as a framework for this exhibition, and what meanings does it hold in the work?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, I was thinking about the landscape as both a physical environment and a metaphor for those interconnected systems of support, protection, and transformation. Mangroves are environments that resist simple definitions. They exist between land and water, constantly negotiating changing conditions, yet they support incredibly complex systems of life. The roots intertwine, creating structures that offer protection and stability while allowing other forms of life to flourish. Could this offer another way of considering how cultural traditions endure? article_text:
At Pérez Art Museum Miami, Anina Major’s ‘The Sacred Mangrove’ explores Bahamian cultural heritage, ancestral knowledge and the relationship between material traditions and contemporary sculpture.

What happens when the knowledge carried through generations is transformed into something new? In ‘The Sacred Mangrove ‘ , Bahamian artist Anina Major reimagines traditional palm weaving through monumental ceramic sculptures, creating an immersive landscape that considers memory, migration and cultural continuity. Drawing on the plaiting practices passed down by her grandmother, Major challenges the distinctions between craft and fine art while questioning how cultural value is assigned and preserved. Through woven clay structures, bottle trees and references to Caribbean ecologies, the exhibition examines the relationships between ancestry, labour, spirituality and belonging.

In conversation with ART AFRICA , Major reflects on the enduring intelligence of traditional practices, the complexities of representing Bahamian identity, and how cultural knowledge continues to evolve across generations and geographies. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

Brendon Bell-Roberts: At the centre of ‘The Sacred Mangrove’ is your transformation of weaving from an organic, flexible practice into one shaped through fired clay. What becomes possible when you translate a material tradition associated with impermanence into something enduring?

Anina Major: I find the relationship between permanence and impermanence fascinating because neither material is entirely one or the other. Palm is organic and eventually biodegrades, while clay begins soft and vulnerable before undergoing an extraordinary transformation through fire. It becomes permanent, yet remains fragile. Initially, working with clay was a way of maintaining a connection to my grandmother after her passing. I was watching the few straw objects she left behind slowly deteriorate, and I became curious about what might happen if I translated those gestures into another material. What emerged was more than a way of preserving a form. Clay introduced its own possibilities for scale, structure, and expression. It allowed me to reconsider how we encounter these familiar objects and the value we assign to the knowledge embedded within them. With ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, that exploration has expanded beyond individual sculptures into an entire landscape. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

Weaving carries histories of labour, knowledge and ancestry within Bahamian culture. How do you approach these histories in your practice, especially when working with traditions that continue to evolve across generations?

I grew up understanding plaiting through the women around me, particularly my grandmother. It was part of her everyday life, a skill that required patience, ingenuity, and an incredible understanding of material. As I began researching the practice more deeply, I became interested in how much knowledge was being communicated through the hands. Plaiting is mathematical, structural, economic, and cultural all at once. There are histories embedded in the patterns, but there is also tremendous individuality in how those patterns are interpreted. Every generation makes its own contributions, whether through changes in material, technique, or purpose. My work is another contribution to that ongoing conversation. Anina Major, ‘ Water Tower ‘, 2024. Glazed stoneware, melted sea glass and sand. Collection Pérez Art Museum Miami, museum purchase with funds provided by PAMM’s Collectors Council. Credits to Anina Major. Image Courtesy of artist and Tern Gallery. Photo by Andrew White.

The exhibition considers the relationship between cultural traditions and the Bahamas’ representation within the tourism economy. How has this tension shaped how you think about value, visibility and cultural identity in your work?

Growing up in The Bahamas, tourism was an unavoidable part of how we understood ourselves and how the rest of the world encountered us. The image of paradise is incredibly powerful, but it can also flatten the complexity of a place and the people who inhabit it. A plaited object sold in the Straw Market as a souvenir had the ability to embody extraordinary history and skill. Within another context, the conversation around its value shifts. It’s this discourse that inspired this body of work. Questioning the systems that determine what we celebrate, what we overlook, and whose contributions are recognised. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

Mangroves occupy an important space within Caribbean ecologies, existing between land and water while providing protection, shelter and interconnected systems of life. What drew you to the mangrove as a framework for this exhibition, and what meanings does it hold in the work?

For ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, I was thinking about the landscape as both a physical environment and a metaphor for those interconnected systems of support, protection, and transformation. Mangroves are environments that resist simple definitions. They exist between land and water, constantly negotiating changing conditions, yet they support incredibly complex systems of life. The roots intertwine, creating structures that offer protection and stability while allowing other forms of life to flourish. Could this offer another way of considering how cultural traditions endure? They don’t necessarily survive by remaining unchanged, but through adaptation, exchange, and the relationships that sustain them. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

The installation brings together towering woven clay forms, bottle trees, crushed conch shells and Water Tower . How do these objects and materials speak to one another within the exhibition space?

I see the exhibition as a landscape rather than a collection of individual sculptures. Each element contributes to the environment, and their relationships become just as important as the objects themselves. The woven ceramic structures establish a sense of monumentality, while the bottle trees introduce associations with protection and spiritual practices within the African diaspora. The crushed conch shells and ceramic shards contribute metaphorical meaning that grounds the work beyond a surface upon which the sculptures are displayed. Water Tower draws from a historic landmark in Nassau associated with water and sustenance. Within the exhibition, it takes on another relationship to the surrounding forms. I’m interested in how these different elements begin to create a sense of place without necessarily representing a specific location. Together, they suggest an environment shaped by histories of labour, survival, spirituality, and our relationships with the natural world. Anina Major, ‘ Water Tower ‘, 2024. Glazed stoneware, melted sea glass and sand. Collection Pérez Art Museum Miami, museum purchase with funds provided by PAMM’s Collectors Council. Credits to Anina Major. Image Courtesy of artist and Tern Gallery. Photo by Andrew White.

Your practice moves between categories often described separately as craft, sculpture and installation. How do you understand these distinctions in your own work, and what happens when they overlap?

Rarely, do I think about whether my work belongs to craft, sculpture, or installation while I’m making it. Those distinctions can feel quite restrictive to the creative process. Plaiting carries extraordinary intelligence, yet practices associated with women, domestic labour, or communities outside dominant art histories have often been categorised differently. I’m curious what happens when those hierarchies are challenged, particularly through material and scale. Some of the objects and artworks I admire most blur these distinctions, and history has shown that objects can move between categories depending on who is looking, where they’re presented, and when. My practice has evolved from individual ceramic sculptures toward environments that engage with landscape. I don’t see that as leaving craft behind. Rather, I want to see how far the structural language of plaiting can extend and what new possibilities emerge along the way. Installation view of ‘ Anina Major: The Sacred Mangrove ‘, Pérez Art Museum Miami, 2026. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

Ideas of memory and belonging recur throughout your practice. How has living and working between the Bahamas and New York shaped how you think about place, distance and the preservation or transformation of cultural knowledge?

Leaving The Bahamas made me much more conscious of the ways place shapes our understanding of ourselves. There are things you take for granted when you’re surrounded by them, and distance has a way of bringing those things into focus. But living away also complicates your relationship with home. You change, the place you left changes, and eventually you recognise that returning doesn’t necessarily mean recovering something exactly as you remember it. That experience has influenced how I think about cultural traditions. It may be impossible to preserve something exactly as it was, but how it continues to evolve as people move between places and encounter different influences- well, that’s intriguing. Portrait of Anina Majors. Photo by Lazaro Llanes.

As visitors move physically through ‘ The Sacred Mangrove ‘ , what role does their encounter with the installation’s scale, materiality and spatial arrangement play in how the work unfolds?

Working at a larger scale has fundamentally changed my relationship to the work. With smaller objects, the encounter can be quite intimate. You stand outside the work and observe it. But an environment asks something different of you. You have to physically negotiate the space, moving around and between. In ‘The Sacred Mangrove’, the arrangement of the sculptures, the ground beneath them, and the spaces between them are all part of the experience. The viewer’s body becomes a measure of the work, and their movement changes with what they notice.

This exhibition is on view at the Pérez Art Museum Miami , in Florida, until 1 August 2027.

article_text:
Sponsored by 株式会社NINO

株式会社山田養蜂場 が主催するアートフェスティバル 「みつばち芸術祭 ―Be(e) the Future ミツバチと共に描く、生命の未来―」 が、学生を対象にした彫刻作品の公募を行っている。募集期間は11月30日23:59まで。

2027年9月18日～11月23日に、岡山県苫田郡の山田養蜂場敷地内で開催される「みつばち芸術祭 ―Be(e) the Future ミツバチと共に描く、生命の未来―」は、創業以来、「自然との調和」を理念に持続可能な社会作りと環境保全に取り組む山田養蜂場が手がける芸術祭。「循環と共生」の象徴としてのミツバチをイベント名に冠し、アートディレクターには 長谷川祐子 を迎えている。プログラムは、招待アーティストによるコミッションワーク、学生を対象とした公募による展示をはじめとするイベントで構成。展示作品は彫刻のみで、すべて山田養蜂場本社の敷地内に屋外展示される。

今回の公募は、「ミツバチ」を出発点に、生命や自然との新たな関係を彫刻でかたちにする、学生のための企画。全国の大学・大学院・短期大学・専門学校・高校等に在籍し、美術・芸術・デザイン・建築・空間演出等を学ぶ学生・研究生が対象となる。採択予定数は5作品で、本芸術祭のテーマに沿ったサイト・スペシフィックな彫刻作品を募る。採用された作品には、1作品につき上限300万円を目安とした制作委託費が支給される。

審査員を務めるのは、 山田英生 （株式会社山田養蜂場 代表取締役社長）、 長谷川祐子 （キュレーター、近現代美術史、京都大学・ヴェネチア大学客員教授）、 名和晃平 （彫刻家、Sandwich Inc.主宰、京都芸術大学教授）、 AKI INOMATA （アーティスト、武蔵野美術大学彫刻学科客員教授）、 板垣李光人 （俳優、スターダストプロモーション）、 佐々木正己 （玉川大学名誉教授）、 五木田聡 （株式会社山田養蜂場 顧問、前・東京富士美術館館長）の7名。審査は、書類による一次審査と、東京で行う模型とプレゼンテーションによる最終審査の2段階で実施される。

長谷川祐子は本公募にあたり、 「ミツバチのしなやかな身体、光を透かす翅、群れが描く軌跡。六角形が限りなく連なるハニカムの巣、花粉を運び蜜を醸す営み、数万の個体がひとつの生命体のように呼吸するコロニーの知性。ミツバチの姿や生態、巣のかたちなど、ミツバチから受け取ったイメージを出発点に、自由で、生命力にあふれた造形を期待しています。写実である必要はありません。抽象でも、構造体でも、風や光を受けとめる装置でもかまいません」 とのメッセージを寄せている。

募集要項などの詳細は、 公式サイト で確認してほしい。

article_text:
The harrowing but ultimately hopeful story of the FlyDubai airline hijacking incident last month is being developed as a narrative film by Dori Media Group and India’s Sphereorigin .

The Sept. 30 incident is believed to have been a terror plot by the co-pilot of the FlyDubai plane that was bound for Ben-Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv. The flight was primarily full of Israeli citizens traveling home after visiting in Dubai. The co-pilot is alleged to have stabbed the plane’s captain and taken over the flight controls with the intention of crashing it into Ben-Gurion airport. The flight is reported to have plummeted more than 14,000 feet for about 30 seconds until valiant efforts by the injured pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, allowed passengers to overpower the suspected pilot in the cockpit.

Related Stories

Appetite for Agatha Christie Shows No Signs of Slowing 50 Years After Her Death: 'She Has Such Enduring Appeal'

The extraordinary circumstances have turned Machchhar into a national hero in his native India as well as in Israel. Dori Media, which produces film and TV out of Tel Aviv, Zurich and Buenos Aires, was approached by representatives for Sphereorigin about working together on a film. The project came together in record time in old-school fashion at the Mipcom content market and conference in Cannes.

“We were approached by streaming platforms and broadcasters in India expressing interest to tell the heroic story of the Indian pilot and the courageous Israeli passengers on that recent flight,” said Sunjoy Waddhwa, managing director at Mumbai-based Sphereorigins. “We are privileged to collaborate with Dori Media on this premium project as we have known and worked with them for a long time and together with Subh (Subhadarshi Tripathy) felt they’d be the ideal partner to produce a film of this caliber.”

Tripathy brokered the deal on behalf of Dori Media and Sphereorigin.

Dori Media chief Nadav Palti was surprised and energized to get a phone call from the parties on Oct. 11, on the eve of Mipcom opening. The sides met in the Dori Media booth at the Palais and hammered out the terms of the development pact by the afternoon of Oct. 14. Palti told Variety the speed of the deal coming together indicated the desire by the companies to tell the story of the incident that could have been a devastating tragedy but instead became a triumph that demonstrated the skill and the courage of Machchhar, who is recovering from his injuries. The co-pilot accused of carrying out the attack is under arrest and facing prosecution by UAE authorities.

“We are honored to jointly produce this special film with the team at Sphereorigins,” said Palti. “What happened on that flight was nothing short of a miracle and we will approach this film by looking to tell the heroic story of the pilot and those brave passengers who helped save the lives of many aboard that historic flight.”

In the narrative that has unfolded from authorities and passenger accounts, Machchhar had the presence of mind to open the locked door of the cockpit after he was stabbed. That allowed passengers to hear the commotion and discover what was happening. Machchhar tried to fight to retain control of the plane and amid that noise, a group of passengers were able to subdue the suspected assailant. Two other pilots who happened to be traveling on the flight then took over and were able to safely land the plane at the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The ability to do so marked a gesture of kindness from the Saudi kingdom that does not otherwise allow Israel-affiliated aircraft to land within its borders.

“I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside,” Machchhar said recently in a highly publicized video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. “I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die.”

Waddhwa moved to strike a film development deal around the incident after getting unsolicited inquiries from Indian media firms. The partners are still looking for a writer and a director. The hope is to release the movie on an accelerated timetable next year, likely on a streaming platform.

“We were approached by streaming platforms and broadcasters in India expressing interest to tell the heroic story of the Indian pilot and the courageous Israeli passengers on that recent flight,” Waddhwa said. “We are privileged to collaborate with Dori Media on this premium project as we have known and worked with them for a long time and together with Subh (Subhadarshi Tripathy) felt they’d be the ideal partner to produce a film of this caliber.”

Sphereorigin was founded by Waddhwa and others in 2002. Dori Media Group has grown to rank among Israel’s largest independent producers since its launch in 1996. The company had its largest slate of offerings — from documentary features and docuseries to game and competition series to scripted dramas — at Mipcom. It produces a wide slate of Spanish-language content for Argentina and other Latin American markets.
